solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Party leads to some sleep deprivation — have kip wherever suits

indicators.note: the leads of the next words are their first letters

parts.note: first letters of some, sleep, deprivation

explanation.surface: A party that leads to sleep loss, so guests nap wherever they can.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash hides where the definition starts: 'have' is wordplay, and 'kip wherever suits' is the definition. Kip is British slang for sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: To doss down is to bed down for the night in whatever makeshift place is available.

clue.text: Having dreadful ado, counts old silver coins

indicators.note: the letters of the fodder are in a dreadful state, so rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone making a fuss while counting an old coin collection.
explanation.walkthrough: A ducatoon was a silver coin of 17th-century Italy and the Low Countries, a larger cousin of the ducat.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical term: the ducatoon was a silver coin once current in Italy and the Low Countries.

clue.text: Husband cutting pig up in display

indicators.note: the husband cuts into the pig, so sits inside it

parts.note: a sow is a female pig
as with a race that is up and running, the runners are off

explanation.surface: A husband carving up a pig in front of an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The pig is SOW, not HOG, and 'up' is not a reversal here but a word of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrasal-verb synonym: to parade something so others admire it is to display it.

clue.text: Bores medic with misfortunes

explanation.surface: A doctor who tediously bores everyone with tales of woe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' reads as a noun for tedious people, but it is the verb: to make holes.
explanation.definitionFit: To drill is to bore a hole.

clue.text: Before permission to act, decree resolution

indicators.note: the decree comes before the permission

parts.note: a will is a decree or command

explanation.surface: A legal decree being resolved once authority to act is granted.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is written back to front: the first piece named, 'permission to act', goes second.
explanation.definitionFit: Willpower is resolution, the determination to carry something through.

clue.text: Historian VIP boastfully backtracks

indicators.note: the whole string goes back the way it came

parts.note: a nob is a toff, a bigwig

explanation.surface: A pompous dignitary retreating from something he boasted about.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Gibbon wrote The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire; 'Historian' could also be a monkey in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Gibbon was the 18th-century English historian.

clue.text: Avarice besetting fringes of The Met

indicators.note: greed surrounds the other letters
the fringes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Greed surrounding the Metropolitan Opera or the Met Police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Met' looks like one name, but only 'The' is wordplay; 'Met' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: welcoming someone on arrival is meeting them.

clue.text: Café from Egon Ronay initially in club

indicators.note: take the initial letters of Egon Ronay

parts.note: a brassie is an old golf club, a wooden two-wood

indicators.note: those letters go inside the club

explanation.surface: A café recommended by the famous restaurant guide, found in a club.
explanation.walkthrough: Egon Ronay was a food critic whose guides rated British restaurants, which suits the café surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: the French word for an informal restaurant serving simple food and drink, much like a café.

clue.text: Such unity could make no sense

indicators.note: the fodder's letters could be made into the answer

explanation.surface: A cynic's remark that such perfect unity makes no sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such' points on to the answer: unity of the kind this anagram produces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the state of being one whole is unity, and 'such' points at the answer as its kind.

clue.text: Expanded odourless gas that's odd

indicators.note: the formula is written out in full, the 2 becoming a second O

parts.note: carbon dioxide, whose formula has one carbon and two oxygens

explanation.surface: A puzzled note about an odourless gas that has expanded.
explanation.walkthrough: Carbon dioxide is CO2; 'expanded' writes the second oxygen out. 'Coo!' is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Coo!' is what you say when something strikes you as odd.

clue.text: Ignorant, stupid, endless repeat

indicators.note: the word loses both its ends

parts.note: SILLY without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A string of insults: ignorant, stupid, the same thing over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' could clip only the last letter; here SILLY loses both ends to give ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Illiterate can mean ignorant in general, not only unable to read.

clue.text: Writer wants time cut in part

indicators.note: the cut goes inside the part

explanation.surface: An author wanting a time cut in his part.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire books.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Victorian novelist Anthony Trollope, author of the Barsetshire books.

clue.text: Decoration left on piece of armour plate

indicators.note: in an across clue, left is added on after the armour

parts.note: a tasse is a plate of armour guarding the thigh

explanation.surface: An ornament left on a suit of armour.
explanation.walkthrough: The obscure part is the armour: a tasse (or tace) is one of the overlapping plates hanging below the breastplate.
explanation.definitionFit: A tassel is a decorative tuft of threads.

clue.text: Former king leading away from answer

indicators.note: the first piece leads, coming before the second

explanation.surface: A deposed monarch leading people away from an answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was the 8th-century king of Mercia, famous for Offa's Dyke on the Welsh border.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Anglo-Saxon ruler of Mercia, who died in 796.

clue.text: Skill needs past struggling

indicators.note: the letters thrash about into a new order

explanation.surface: A struggler told that acquiring skill takes getting past something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needs past' reads as grammar in the surface, but those two words are exactly the letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: being adept at something means having skill in it.

clue.text: Bearing ordinary pot plant

explanation.surface: An ordinary potted plant bearing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot plant' looks like a houseplant; 'pot' is cannabis, which is also grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Sword grass is a grass or sedge with sharp, blade-like leaves.

clue.text: Again investigate case of rogue despot once found in river

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters

parts.note: first and last letters of ROGUE

indicators.note: the despot is found inside the river

parts.note: the Exe, a river in Devon
Idi Amin, former dictator of Uganda

explanation.surface: A fresh inquiry into a rogue former dictator discovered in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Idi Amin ruled Uganda in the 1970s, hence 'despot once'; the Exe runs through Exeter in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with the prefix doing the work of 'again': to look into something a second time.

clue.text: Brazen criminal hassles me

indicators.note: the letters are criminally mistreated, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a brazen crook keeps pestering the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brazen criminal' reads as one phrase, but 'Brazen' is the definition and 'criminal' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone brazen acts boldly with no sense of shame.

clue.text: Rose finally seduces number one bachelor in German city

indicators.note: the bachelor goes inside the city
take the final letter of seduces

parts.note: 'number one' is a nursery euphemism for a wee

explanation.surface: Rose at last seduces the leading bachelor in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name; it is the flower. 'Number one' is not first place but a child's word for a wee.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: eglantine, a European wild rose with fragrant leaves.

clue.text: Most of timber on northern island suitable for court?

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter, so the timber is cut short
in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

explanation.surface: Timber on a northern island that might be fit for a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court or a tennis court; the question mark signals the old sense of courting, or wooing.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wooable is fit to be courted.

clue.text: Ring secures inverted support gear used in lift?

indicators.note: the ring holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: to ring is to bell, a call on the phone

indicators.note: the support is turned upside down, reading upwards

parts.note: a bra is a support garment

explanation.surface: A ring holding a support upside down in a lift mechanism.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'lift' as weightlifting rather than an elevator.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbell is the bar of weights used in weightlifting.

clue.text: Two books, each absorbing day after day

indicators.note: each takes the days inside it

explanation.surface: Two books each absorbing the reader day after day.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two Eddas, the Elder (Poetic) and the Younger (Prose), collections of Old Norse writing.
explanation.definitionFit: The Edda is the name shared by two Icelandic books of Norse myth and poetry.

clue.text: One destined to serve picked up drink and MDMA

indicators.note: what is picked up is heard, so the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a draught is a drink; E is ecstasy, the drug MDMA

explanation.surface: A conscript caught with a drink and ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: Draught is the British spelling for a drink from the barrel; said aloud it sounds like the American DRAFT.
explanation.definitionFit: A draftee is someone conscripted for military service.

clue.text: Fungus source beginning to rot in huge borders of grass

indicators.note: take the beginning of rot
that letter goes inside huge
the borders of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Where mushrooms spring up: rot among huge grassy margins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fungus' is not a mushroom but Fungus the Bogeyman, the picture book by Raymond Briggs, who is its source.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Briggs created Fungus the Bogeyman.

clue.text: First sign of jungle animal's pad

indicators.note: take the first letter of jungle

parts.note: the otter, with 's as the link 'is'

explanation.surface: The first trace of a jungle beast's paw print, or its lair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pad' could be an animal's paw or home; here it is a notepad. The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, mainly British: a small book of paper for jotting notes on is a pad.

clue.text: Attitude in estate, maybe one overwhelmed by anger

indicators.note: an estate is one example of a car

parts.note: an estate is a type of car, a station wagon

indicators.note: the one is swallowed up by the anger, so sits inside it

explanation.surface: A stance adopted on a country estate by someone consumed by fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Estate' suggests land; in Britain an estate is also a car with a large boot, called a station wagon elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Carriage is posture, the way one holds oneself, which is one sense of attitude.

clue.text: English look back into human form of cultivation?

indicators.note: to look back is to face the way you came, so the word for look is read in reverse
both pieces go inside the human

explanation.surface: An Englishman peering back into how people cultivate things.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags an odd definition: bees are kept and cultivated rather than crops.
explanation.definitionFit: Beekeeping is a form of husbandry, cultivating bees for honey.

clue.text: Traitorous secret agents progressively picked out letter

indicators.note: take letter one of the first word, letter two of the second, letter three of the third

explanation.surface: Double agents gradually exposed by an intercepted letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked out' suggests taking first letters; 'progressively' moves one letter further along in each word.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword-friendly sense: letters have spelt-out names, and the twentieth letter's name is written this way.

clue.text: Receptacle, somewhat useless, eventually returned

indicators.note: only part of the words is used
those letters read back the other way

parts.note: the run of letters inside useLESS EVentually

explanation.surface: A container that proved rather useless and was eventually sent back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat' is easy to read as a hedge on 'useless'; it is the signal that the answer sits inside the next words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a jug, bowl or cask is a container for holding liquid.

clue.text: Revise opinion on fools — simpletons, primarily

indicators.note: take the first letter of simpletons

explanation.surface: Changing one's mind about fools, who are mainly simpletons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is not a link here but RE, the memo word for 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: judging something afresh is revising your view of it.
